title: Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co.
summary: A log-driving contract was divisible by completed deliveries at specified unit prices, but the contractor could not collect a fraction of a delivery price for logs lost partway through the journey.
notes: Citation and rule statement: Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co., 151 Pa. 534, 25 A. 120 (1892); a contract is severable (divisible) when one party's performance consists of several distinct items and the price is apportioned to each item, so payment is due per unit actually delivered.

sections.Parties: Gill agreed to drive logs and railroad ties to specified destinations. Johnstown Lumber was to pay for those deliveries.
sections.Material Facts:
The contract covered roughly four million feet of logs and required work to begin at once, using natural water or splash dams. Payment varied by item: one dollar per thousand feet of oak logs, seventy-five cents per thousand feet of other logs, three cents per tie delivered to Bethel, and five cents per tie delivered farther downstream.

A catastrophic flood carried many logs past the company’s boom. Some had been driven part of the way by Gill and others had not been touched. Other logs and ties had been successfully delivered to the places the contract specified. The contract apportioned prices to types and destinations, but did not apportion a price to separate portions of each journey.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court directed a verdict for the lumber company because it considered the contract entire and Gill’s failure to deliver the whole quantity fatal to recovery. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed and ordered a new trial.
sections.Issue: Was full performance of the entire contract a condition of all compensation, and could payment be apportioned either by delivered items or by distance traveled?
sections.Holding: Gill could recover the stipulated rates for logs and ties actually delivered at the specified destinations. He could not recover proportional compensation for undelivered logs merely because he had moved them partway.
sections.Reasoning:
Distinct performances paired with apportioned prices made the contract severable. Failure as to one delivery did not erase the agreed payment for another completed delivery. The court compared carriage cases in which a stated rate supported payment for the cargo actually delivered despite a shortfall in the total shipment.

The unit of division still mattered. Each log’s whole journey had a single price tied to delivery at its destination. There was no basis to divide that price among miles or stages. Divisibility therefore preserved earned portions of compensation while retaining the completion condition for each unit.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Divisibility asks which parts of an exchange the agreement treats as corresponding units. It can reduce forfeiture without rewriting every unfinished task into a payable fraction.

topics.conditions: Completion remains required for each unit even though the whole contract need not be completed.
topics.divisibility: Separate item prices support payment for distinct completed deliveries.
topics.forfeiture: Earned compensation for delivered items survives a failure elsewhere in the contract.
topics.interpretation: The allocation of prices determines the appropriate unit of performance.
topics.constructive-conditions: The entire-versus-severable analysis decides whether full performance is a constructive condition of any payment, which is how the trial court had ruled before reversal.
topics.risk-allocation: The flood placed the loss on whoever the contract's price structure left unpaid for the lost logs, so the case shows a court allocating a casualty loss through construction of the payment terms.
